title: Jean Baudrillard
summary: Jean Baudrillard was a French sociologist and philosopher who studied consumer society and the media. His central idea: images and copies increasingly replace reality — these are “simulacra,” copies without an original — until “hyperreality” emerges, a world where the image seems more real than the world itself. He wrote provocatively and rather darkly, but his view helps you notice how much of what you feel has been shaped by screens and shop windows.
onEmotions: Baudrillard built no theory of emotions and was skeptical of “psychology.” But an important thought follows from his ideas: many feelings today pass through simulacra — images of happiness from advertising, rehearsed emotions on social media, the “right” feelings from TV series. In The Consumer Society he showed that we buy things as signs of status and identity, not only for their use — and the same happens with moods. His view is uncomfortable, but freeing: if your feeling doesn't match the glossy picture, perhaps it is the picture that is wrong, not you. It is worth looking not for the “ideal” emotion but for the one that remains when the screen is switched off.

anxiety.text: Back in 1983, long before smartphones, Baudrillard described the “ecstasy of communication”: everything visible, everything available, the flow of messages never stopping, day or night. Anxiety with no clear cause often lives right here. In such an environment a person loses their protective distance — they become a “screen” through which other people's news, opinions and disasters pass. Baudrillard would probably note that part of your anxiety is not a personal malfunction but a natural reaction to a surplus of signals that cannot be digested. This doesn't mean your anxiety is “not real.” But it helps to tell apart the anxiety about what is happening to you and the anxiety the screen brings. The second kind can sometimes be eased simply by closing the flow for a while.
anxiety.practice: Turn off your phone's screen and look into its black glass for a minute, until your reflection and the room appear in it. Then ask: what worries me here, in this room, rather than in the feed?

fear.text: In 1991 Baudrillard published a provocative piece, “The Gulf War Did Not Take Place” — not denying the bombs, but showing that for most viewers the war existed as a television spectacle. Your fear deserves respect: it is an ancient protector. But it is worth looking at where it came from. Disasters and threats are shown so often and so spectacularly that they become “hyperreality” — an image that feels more real than the everyday life outside your window. Baudrillard also wrote about the logic of “deterrence”: modern systems rest less on events than on their constant possibility, always looming on the horizon. Take Baudrillard's thought one step further, and it turns out that we live through many fears “in simulation” — again and again, before anything has actually happened. Recognizing this doesn't mean dismissing the danger. It helps you return to the concrete: what threatens me in particular, right now, and what is within my power?
fear.practice: Imagine your fear as a film and ask which shots you filmed yourself, with your own eyes, and which were edited in from screens and hearsay. In your mind, keep only your own footage.

sadness.text: “Melancholy is the fundamental tonality of systems of simulation,” Baudrillard writes: as meanings multiply, get copied and lose their value, there seems to be more of everything around — and less of anything real. If sadness descends for no visible reason, that doesn't make you “ungrateful.” Baudrillard would probably note that your sadness may be a sensitive response not only to something personal but to this shared “faded” atmosphere, where even feelings come prepackaged. That doesn't make sadness an illness. It is more a sign of living receptiveness. Baudrillard writes no prescriptions for cheerfulness — he suggests not pretending. Allowing yourself to be sad without a “positive” filter is already a small way out of the simulation.
sadness.practice: Sit for five minutes in half-darkness with no music and no screen — improving nothing, not turning the sadness into “content.” Just let it be, unfiltered.

grief.text: The cemetery once stood at the very center of the village, by the church, Baudrillard recalls in Symbolic Exchange and Death — and then it was moved beyond the city limits. Our culture treats grief, in which nothing actually needs “fixing,” the same way: it pushes loss to the margins — hides it, hurries it, gives it less and less room in shared life. In traditional cultures, he says, the living continued an “exchange” with the departed: through rituals, gifts, memory, conversation. We, by contrast, often expect a grieving person to “get back to normal” quickly. Your grief doesn't have to adapt to that pace. You can keep a bond with whoever or whatever you have lost: remember, talk, make small ritual gestures. This is how you recover something our culture has forgotten how to do.
grief.practice: Make a small exchange with the one who is gone: place an apple, a flower or a cup of tea by their photo and silently say what you have brought today.

loneliness.text: A hundred messages a day — and not one person in the room: Baudrillard saw this not as an accident but as the design of the age, and that is exactly why loneliness amid endless communication hurts. He called it the paradox of the “ecstasy of communication”: connections multiply, messages fly nonstop, but the encounter itself — presence, silence shared by two, a look — is more and more often replaced by its simulation. Baudrillard might say that a reaction under a post resembles attention, a chat resembles a conversation, a feed resembles your friends' lives. And your loneliness may be not a sign that something is wrong with you, but an accurate sense of the difference between the sign of closeness and closeness itself. That sense is a valuable sensitivity. It suggests that what you need is not another portion of contact, but a different kind of it — slow, bodily, imperfect, without an audience.
loneliness.practice: Call someone by voice rather than by message — even for three minutes. Listen to the pauses and the breathing on the other end: messaging doesn't have them.

anger.text: A Che Guevara portrait on a T-shirt from a shopping mall is an almost ready-made illustration of Baudrillard. Your anger is honest and has its reasons, but the system knows how to absorb protest and hand it back as a commodity: critique becomes content, outrage becomes a reason to click. Hence a particular anger with no outlet: it seems that even your rage has already been built into someone's shop window. It seems that it isn't worth handing your anger over to be recycled into yet another spectacle. He himself responded to the world with irony and provocation rather than head-on confrontation. You can acknowledge anger, feel it in your body and direct it into a real conversation or action — where it changes something, rather than just collecting views.
anger.practice: Clench your fists as hard as you can for ten seconds, feel the anger in your whole body — and slowly let go. Then ask: who is my anger really addressed to, once the audience is gone?

shame.text: An ad for face cream with skin smooth as plastic shows, Baudrillard would say, not a person but a model: it has no wrinkles because it has no life. If you feel ashamed of your body, looks or way of life next to such images, it is not your fault. In The Consumer Society Baudrillard called the body “the finest consumer object”: the body is turned into a project to be constantly improved, invested in, displayed. The standards, meanwhile, are set by edited images — simulacra that have no living original. Baudrillard would probably note that shame arises when a living, changing person compares themselves to a copy without an original. It is an unfair competition. Understanding this logic doesn't dissolve shame at once, but it changes its meaning: you are not “falling short” — you are measuring yourself against something that doesn't actually exist.
shame.practice: Look at your hand in ordinary daylight: veins, creases, marks. Tell it silently: “You are not a picture — you are alive.”

guilt.text: “Have fun!” sounds like an invitation at first, but Baudrillard heard an order in it. Hence a strange guilt when you haven't harmed anyone and are simply not happy, productive or “positive” enough. In The Consumer Society Baudrillard wrote about “fun-morality” (he used the English phrase): in a society of abundance, pleasure becomes a duty. You are supposed to enjoy yourself, try new things, rest “properly” — and if it doesn't work out, it feels as if you've broken a rule. For Baudrillard, such guilt is not the voice of conscience but the inner supervisor of consumer society. A simple question helps tell one from the other: whom have I harmed? If no one — perhaps you are “guilty” only before an advertising image of a happy life, and you owe it nothing.
guilt.practice: Ask your guilt aloud: “Show me whom I hurt.” If there's no answer, calmly add: “Then you're not my conscience, you're an advert” — and let it go for the evening.

envy.text: Why does the neighbor's car suddenly seem necessary, when yours runs perfectly well? Baudrillard answered without moralizing: envy is largely produced by the very environment we live in, and it is a very human feeling. In The System of Objects and The Consumer Society Baudrillard showed that we acquire things not only for their use but for their “sign value” — what they say about our place among others. A need, for Baudrillard, is often a need not for the thing itself but for difference: to be no worse, to be more visible. Such a system is never satisfied, because a new mark of distinction will always appear. For him, envy is not your moral flaw but a programmed effect of this race. Once the mechanism is visible, envy becomes less personal, and you can ask: what do I really want, and what is merely a sign for standing out?
envy.practice: Imagine the object of your envy becomes yours, but no one will ever know. Listen: do you still want it?

emptiness.text: Simulacra and Simulation opens with a fable by Borges: the empire's cartographers drew a map at full scale, and it covered the entire territory. The emptiness that drains the taste out of life is no small thing, and Baudrillard offered an unexpected explanation for it: he describes a world where copies, images and models gradually push reality aside, leaving “the desert of the real” — there is a lot of everything, yet nothing truly touches you. We are surrounded by pictures of food, travel, love, and it is their very excess that can leave us hungry. In other words, your emptiness may be an honest response to life among simulacra — and so evidence that you need something real. It is not a verdict but a compass. The real is usually humbler than the image: a warm cup in your hands, a living voice, footsteps on a street.
emptiness.practice: Right now, find one sensation that can't be photographed: the temperature of the air, the weight of your body, a sound. Stay with it for a minute.

confusion.text: “We live in a world where there is more and more information, and less and less meaning” — so begins one chapter of Simulacra and Simulation. Confusion before a world that changes faster than it can be understood is almost inevitable here. Baudrillard wrote about the “implosion of meaning” in the media (an implosion is an explosion directed inward): there is more and more information, but instead of clarifying meaning it dissolves it. Every event immediately gathers a thousand interpretations, refutations and jokes — and it is no longer clear what actually happened. Your confusion is not a sign of stupidity or of being unable to cope. It is a reasonable response to an environment where the line between the real and its image is blurred. What helps may be not more information but less: relying on what you know from your own experience, and the right to say, “I don't know yet.”
confusion.practice: Pick one news story that confuses you and decide not to read anything more about it until tomorrow. Today, lean only on what you know firsthand.

quote.text: We live in a world where there is more and more information, and less and less meaning.
quote.author: Jean Baudrillard
quote.source: Simulacra and Simulation (1981), “The Implosion of Meaning in the Media”

fatigue.text: In a book about abundance — The Consumer Society, 1970 — Baudrillard devoted a whole section to fatigue, and it reads as if it were about today's burnout. Your tiredness is not a flaw of character. He noticed that in the society of abundance a strange, “causeless” fatigue spreads, one that physical labor cannot explain. And he offered a bold reading: such fatigue may be a hidden form of resistance — a quiet, bodily refusal of constant mobilization, of the demand to keep producing, consuming and staying on top form. If so, your burnout is not only a personal failure but a signal your body sends instead of words: “I can't go on like this.” That signal deserves to be heard, not drowned out by yet another “efficient” recovery technique.
fatigue.practice: Lie on the floor or the sofa for five minutes and produce nothing: don't listen, don't plan, don't “recover efficiently.” Just let your body refuse.

boredom.text: “What Are You Doing After the Orgy?” — Baudrillard gave one of his essays this title. Boredom amid endless entertainment can be very heavy, and he has an answer as to why. Baudrillard described our time as the state “after the orgy”: everything has already been liberated, permitted, made available, shown — and that is precisely why desire loses its tension. When any film and any music are in your pocket, choosing stops being exciting. Baudrillard would probably note that boredom is not your shortcoming but a natural effect of oversaturation. Treating it with even more content is useless — it only prolongs the “after the orgy.” Sometimes boredom asks for the opposite: limits, pauses, mystery. What isn't available right away becomes interesting again. In this sense boredom is not an emptiness inside you, but desire's longing for the distance that was taken from it.
boredom.practice: Choose one thing — a film, an album, a book — and set it aside until tomorrow without opening it. Notice how your attitude to it changes while you wait.

quote.text: If I were asked to characterize the present state of affairs, I would describe it as “after the orgy.”
quote.author: Jean Baudrillard

joy.text: A child jumping in puddles produces nothing and proves nothing — Baudrillard would call this the world of play and seduction. Your joy, too, needs neither proof nor justification. Baudrillard criticized the “happiness industry” a great deal — advertising smiles, compulsory leisure, joy as a commodity. But he was no enemy of pleasure. In Seduction he contrasts the world of production, where everything must yield a result, with the world of play, appearances, ritual and lightness. Seduction, for Baudrillard, is a game in which nothing needs to be accumulated or proven. Take Baudrillard's thought one step further, and it turns out that real joy is closer to play than to achievement. It doesn't have to become a photo, a post or a “result.” Let your joy stay a little unproductive and a little secret — that way it stays yours for longer.
joy.practice: Live through one joy today without showing it or telling anyone about it. How is it different from a joy that gets shared?

love.text: A veil, a half-shadow, a sentence broken off midway — Baudrillard thought desire lives precisely where not everything is shown. That is how he defended love and tenderness: through the value of secrecy. He criticized the culture of total transparency, where everything must be shown, spelled out, put on display; he called such transparency “obscene,” because it destroys the distance in which desire lives. In Seduction he writes about the play of appearances and things left unsaid, about the fact that the other is never fully revealed. It follows that tenderness needs a little shadow. Not every feeling has to be explained and published. Your love doesn't become smaller because others don't see it; sometimes it is precisely secrecy that keeps it alive.
love.practice: Make one small gesture of tenderness today without explaining or photographing it: leave an unsigned note, straighten a blanket, let a glance linger.

gratitude.text: The potlatch — a feast where a chief gave wealth away, and the more generous the gift, the stronger the bond — Baudrillard valued above any deal. Gratitude lives by the same logic. Following the anthropologist Marcel Mauss, he contrasted commodity exchange with “symbolic exchange”: gift and counter-gift, a bond that can't be reduced to a price. In the commodity world everything can be bought and returned, and once accounts are settled nobody owes anybody anything. In symbolic exchange, a gift creates a relationship and a continuation. In other words, gratitude is a small exit from the logic of the market. When you give thanks not for a service but for presence, attention, for what cannot be paid for, you restore to yourself and to the other the part of life that isn't for sale. It is enough to answer such a gift — with a word, with time, with a small gesture.
gratitude.practice: Today, answer one gift that can't be paid for with a small counter-gift: a cup of tea, some help, a minute of full attention. Don't call it “thanks for the service.”

hope.text: Even the darkest philosopher of simulation has an unexpectedly hopeful thought — and it is about clues. In The Perfect Crime he writes about “the murder of reality” — the attempt to replace the world with its flawless, fully calculated copy. And he notes that this crime is never perfect. Traces, accidents, illusions always remain — something that slips out of control. The world does not yield to total simulation. Baudrillard might say that hope lives precisely in these remainders — in the unpredictable, in what fits neither a forecast nor an algorithm. Not everything is decided in advance. Reality resists, and this stubbornness of the world is a good foundation for hope.
hope.practice: Go outside and within five minutes find three things no one planned: a crack, a bird, an overheard conversation. They are evidence that the world hasn't been fully calculated.

nostalgia.text: “When the real is no longer what it used to be, nostalgia assumes its full meaning,” Baudrillard writes in Simulacra and Simulation. Your tender, aching feeling is part of this story. Baudrillard noticed that in the age of simulation nostalgia becomes especially strong: as reality is increasingly replaced by copies, we are drawn to what once seemed authentic. Hence the fashion for “retro,” vintage filters, endless reissues — the past, too, becomes a commodity and an image. Following Baudrillard, you can distinguish two nostalgias: a bought one — for a stylized “past” that never existed — and a living one — for particular people, places, smells. The first is easy to manipulate. The second is honest and speaks of your values. Don't be ashamed of nostalgia — just ask: do I miss what actually was, or a beautiful picture of it?
nostalgia.practice: Take one nostalgic memory and remove its “filter”: what ordinary, uncomfortable details were there too? What stays precious even with them?

quote.text: When the real is no longer what it used to be, nostalgia assumes its full meaning.
quote.author: Jean Baudrillard
quote.source: Simulacra and Simulation (1981), “The Precession of Simulacra”

craving.text: The question Baudrillard would start with: does a hand reaching for a cigarette, a drink, a phone want the thing, or its promise? A craving can be almost unbearable, and it is nothing to be ashamed of. In The System of Objects Baudrillard described the collector's passion: what keeps a collection moving is not the object already found, but the one still missing. The last item is always ahead — and so desire never closes. In The Consumer Society he added that we want not only the thing but what it signifies — its “sign value”: calm, freedom, belonging, a pause. Baudrillard would probably note that a craving often promises not the thing itself but a sign the thing can never fully deliver anyway. This doesn't make the craving weaker, but it changes the question. Not “how do I defeat it,” but “what sign am I trying to get right now — and is there another way to it?” Meanwhile the wave of craving rises and falls, even if you don't feed it.
craving.practice: When a wave of craving rolls in, name to yourself not the thing but its sign: “right now I want a pause,” “I want freedom.” Breathe slowly while the wave rises and falls.

addiction.text: Why is no amount ever enough? Baudrillard put this question to the whole consumer society, and it applies to any circle built over years around a substance, gambling or a screen — this isn't about “weak willpower.” Baudrillard showed that consumer society works as an endless system of signs: every purchase points to the next, and none brings things to a close, because desire here is aimed not at the object but at difference and promise. Consumption, for Baudrillard, knows no satiation by its very logic. Take Baudrillard's thought one step further, and it turns out that addiction is the same mechanism pushed to its limit and compressed into a single object. It says nothing about you being corrupt; it says how powerfully built the trap is that a great many people fall into. Against this logic Baudrillard set “symbolic exchange” — relationships of the gift, which bind people rather than things. Sometimes the way out of the circle begins exactly like that: with a living connection rather than one more sign.
addiction.practice: Make one symbolic exchange: send a few words to someone around whom you feel lighter — not for the reply, but for the bond. If you feel like it, find a mutual-help group where people talk about the same thing without judgment.

hangover.text: “After the orgy” was Baudrillard's name for our era, but his thought has an everyday side: today any evening leaves a double — photos, videos, messages. Heaviness in the body, anxiety and memory gaps the next morning don't make you a bad person. In the morning it often seems these copies know more about your evening than you do, and your memory gets pieced together from other people's shots. It follows that such a “record” is not the same as what happened. A snapshot tears a second out of context, and anxiety adds the worst possible story to it. You don't have to accept this hyperreal version as the final truth about yourself. You can let your body recover and return to the real: what you know for sure, whom it might be worth calmly messaging, and what is only a picture inflated by shame.
hangover.practice: Put your phone face down and don't open other people's pictures of last night for the next hour. Name aloud three things you remember yourself.

euphoria.text: “Ecstasy” in Baudrillard is not bliss at all: in Fatal Strategies it is a movement that spins on its own, faster and faster, until it loses meaning. Your sudden high, when everything seems possible, is a bright experience you can simply enjoy — but Baudrillard also described another way of going beyond the ordinary. It is “seduction”: play, lightness, appearance, in which nothing needs to be accumulated or proven. In other words, a flash of euphoria is better lived as seduction than as ecstasy — as play rather than as an obligation to keep speeding up. You don't need to turn it into a post, a proof or a plan for the rest of your life. Let it be what it is: a gift of the moment, with a beginning and an end. That is exactly why it is so good.
euphoria.practice: Live this high as play: do something light and useless — spin around, sing a line, toss an apple. No plans for tomorrow.

crash.text: A sparkler burns for a minute, and nobody calls it a fraud because it went out. The drop after a celebration, a success, a vivid evening can be sharp and hurtful, and Baudrillard explained why. In The Consumer Society Baudrillard described the logic of fashion: signs of success and celebration flare up, quickly lose their value and demand replacement. A party, a holiday, an achievement are often lived as such signs — and a sign, for Baudrillard, is short-lived and leaves behind an emptiness that you are immediately offered to fill with something new. Baudrillard might say that the “comedown” is not proof that the joy was fake or that something is wrong with you. It is the moment when the sign has gone out, and life goes on. There's no need to rush to drown the drop with a new high. You can give yourself an ordinary, quiet day — with no celebration and no verdict.
crash.practice: Name one entirely ordinary thing that is still good today: tea, the light in the window, someone's voice. Stay with it for a minute.

panic.text: The “ecstasy of communication,” for Baudrillard, strips a person of protective distance: everything comes too close, everything gets inside. When a wave of panic hits — your heart, your breathing, the sense that something irreparable is about to happen — it is genuinely terrifying, and you are not exaggerating. It seems that in panic the world and the body are experienced exactly like this — with no gap, no “frame,” everything at once and right up close. That's why what helps is whatever restores even a little distance and concreteness: not the image of catastrophe your mind is painting, but the tangible reality around you — the floor, the chair, the air. A wave of panic usually peaks and subsides within a few minutes. While it lasts, it is enough to hold on to the simplest, most real things.
panic.practice: Put both feet on the floor and breathe out more slowly than you breathe in. Then reach out and touch the nearest wall or table — take back distance: here I am, here is the thing, and there is air between us.

dread.text: Baudrillard's last book, published in the year of his death, is called Why Hasn't Everything Already Disappeared? — a question that sounds almost like consolation. When “what is all this for,” the sense of finitude and the abyss, closes in, such a question unexpectedly helps. Baudrillard was a dark thinker, but his later books, such as The Perfect Crime and The Vital Illusion, offer an unexpected foothold. He believed the world never reduces to a final meaning, and he called this the “radical illusion” of the world: reality is not transparent; mystery always remains in it. For him this was not a catastrophe but the condition of being alive: a world fully explained and calculated would be a dead copy. Baudrillard would probably note that the question “what for” gets no final answer not because everything is meaningless, but because the world is larger than any answer. The abyss is this very inexhaustibility. You can look at it not only with fear but with curiosity.
dread.practice: Go to a window and for a minute look at something that exists for no reason at all: a cloud, a branch, light on a wall. Ask not “what for,” but “why is it still here.”

fomo.text: Holidays, weddings, concerts — your friends' feed looks more real than your ordinary Tuesday, and Baudrillard would call it hyperreality. Feeling that everyone lives better while you miss out is painful. Baudrillard gave this feeling a precise language. The feed is a shop window of “hyperreality”: there life appears in selected, edited, spliced-together shots, and those shots seem more real than your own weekdays. For Baudrillard, a simulacrum doesn't necessarily lie — it simply takes the place of what was and begins to set the standard. Take Baudrillard's thought one step further, and it turns out that you are comparing your life from the inside with someone else's life as a sign. It's an unfair comparison from the start — the backstage always loses to the shop window. Your life isn't worse; it just hasn't been edited. And the evening you are “missing” was an ordinary evening for the people there too — with boredom, fatigue and awkwardness that didn't make it into the frame.
fomo.practice: Pick one ordinary minute of today — a queue, the kettle, the walk home — and live it as if it were the only scene that is in nobody's feed.

sleepless.text: At three in the morning the phone screen is the only light in the room, and Baudrillard would probably see in this an exact picture of the era. Insomnia is exhausting, and in the dark everything seems bigger and scarier. Baudrillard wrote that the modern person lives in a state of constant connection: the screen never goes dark, the flow never stops, and the difference between day and night, work and rest, gets erased. It follows that the night could be the last place without signals, but often the screen takes it over too — the feed, the news, unfinished messages. And thoughts in the dark work like the same flow: they replay scenarios that haven't happened and perhaps never will — simulations of the future. You don't need to defeat them. You can just notice that this is replaying, not reality, and give the night back at least a little of its own darkness and quiet.
sleepless.practice: If you can't sleep, turn your phone face down and put it out of reach. Lie in the dark and listen to the night: its sounds need no reply.

betrayal.text: In archaic exchange a gift couldn't simply be returned or thrown away: it bound giver and receiver with an obligation, almost an oath. That is why betrayal wounds so deeply — what collapses is not only trust in a person but the sense that the world is reliable. Following the anthropologist Marcel Mauss, Baudrillard described “symbolic exchange” — relationships held together by gift and response, trust and obligation, which can't be reduced to a transaction. In such relationships every gesture means something and calls for an answer. In other words, betrayal hurts so much precisely because it destroys a symbolic bond, not merely breaks a contract. You gave what cannot be paid for — time, openness, loyalty — and the gift in return never came. Your pain is an accurate measure of the value of what you invested. It says nothing about you being naive. The capacity for symbolic exchange is what makes us human, and there's no need to cancel it because of one rupture.
betrayal.practice: Tell someone you trust one sentence about what happened — not for advice, but so that a bond is alive again in at least one place.

jealousy.text: Night, someone else's phone, a finger above the screen — Baudrillard would recognize his whole theory of transparency in this scene. Jealousy is a burning, very human fear of losing someone dear. Baudrillard wrote a great deal about how our culture demands total transparency: everything must be visible, checked, shown. He called such transparency “obscene,” because it destroys distance, and with it mystery and seduction. In Seduction he insists that another person is never fully revealed, and that this is exactly what makes them desirable. Baudrillard might say that jealousy often pushes toward obscene transparency — to check, to find out, to see everything. But complete visibility brings no peace: behind every answer a new question appears. Accepting that the other is always partly a mystery is painful. But it also means accepting them as a living person, not an object that can be fully controlled.
jealousy.practice: Today, leave one thing about the person you love unknown — don't check, don't ask. Notice what it's like to let the other have a shadow.

resentment.text: What is the price of the injustice done to you? Baudrillard would answer: no currency can cover it. Hence the old grudge — a weight you carry for years and can't put down on command. In his late book Impossible Exchange Baudrillard writes about things that cannot be exchanged for any equivalent. It seems that resentment often rests on exactly this. We wait for compensation — an apology, recognition, punishment — that will balance out the harm done. But some wounds have no equivalent: no word will “give back” what happened. Hence the endless waiting that feeds the grudge. Accepting that the exchange is impossible is bitter, but it can free you: you stop waiting for a payment that won't come, and you no longer have to keep that account. This doesn't mean forgiving or excusing. It means ceasing to be a hostage to waiting and taking your attention back.
resentment.practice: Hold an ordinary coin in your hand for a minute, imagining it is your grudge, the one that can't be exchanged. Then put it in a far drawer: let it lie there, demanding no exchange.

heartbreak.text: Deleting the messages takes one flick of a finger, while the heart needs months: Baudrillard would explain this gap better than most. A broken heart hurts literally, in the body. Baudrillard noticed a feature of our era: everything leaves digital doubles behind. After a breakup a person disappears from your life, but their photos remain, your messages, a profile where life goes on without you. Baudrillard would probably note that you are grieving a real person while also running into their simulacrum, which keeps the loss from coming to an end. The image remains available, but the person does not. It isn't a weakness of yours that it's hard not to look: these copies are designed to draw you in. Often the kindest thing is to put the image at a little distance — not out of revenge and not forever, but so that the real loss can run its course and make room for new life.
heartbreak.practice: Choose one digital shadow of this person — a photo, a chat, a playlist — and put it out of sight for a week, without deleting it. Notice how the air around you changes.

impostor.text: Baudrillard would ask: is there ever a “real” expert without a bit of performance? The fear of being exposed any moment is painful, and it comes even to highly competent people. In Simulacra and Simulation Baudrillard gives a curious example: someone who simulates an illness begins to produce some of its real symptoms — and the line between “true” and “false” blurs. His conclusion is broader: in the modern world, professional roles, statuses and competences largely exist as signs that everyone jointly maintains. Take Baudrillard's thought one step further, and it turns out that the “real expert” you fear you can't measure up to has no inner original either — they too are playing a role and learning as they go. You are not the only pretender in a world of genuine people. You are a person doing the work, and your skill is real exactly to the extent that it works.
impostor.practice: Think of someone you consider a “real pro” and picture their first day at work — lost, pretending to be confident. Smile at them in your mind.

self_hatred.text: Listen closely, Baudrillard would suggest: whose voice does your inner critic use? Sometimes it's an advertising voice-over: “you can do better,” “become a new version of yourself.” Its verdict hurts badly, but it is not the truth about you. In The Consumer Society Baudrillard described how the body and personality are turned into a project to be endlessly improved, with the models for it set by advertising images — copies without a living original. In The Transparency of Evil he spoke of “the hell of the same” — a world where everyone is obliged to coincide with an ideal model of themselves. It follows that the inner critic often speaks in the voice of that model. It compares a living, contradictory person with a simulacrum that doesn't exist. In such a competition anyone would lose. Your failure to match the template is not proof that you are worthless, but a sign that you are real.
self_hatred.practice: Say your inner critic's line aloud in the voice of a shampoo-ad narrator. Listen to how fast it loses weight once its tone is exposed.

helplessness.text: In Fatal Strategies Baudrillard turns the usual picture upside down: we don't steer things; things, events and systems follow their own logic and outplay us. Feeling powerless is hard, especially when you are trying very hard. Baudrillard was skeptical of the idea that an individual steers the world. In Fatal Strategies he suggested looking from the other side: it is not the subject who rules over objects; the world, events and things live by their own logic, and often everything goes differently from what was planned. For Baudrillard this is not a reason for despair but a sobering truth. In other words, your helplessness is largely an honest perception of scale, not a personal failure. Not everything depends on you, and the weight of “I must fix everything” can be eased a little. At the same time the world is unpredictable in both directions: what seems frozen sometimes shifts unexpectedly. Your task is not to control everything but to stay alert to the moment when something becomes possible.
helplessness.practice: Hold any object — a cup, your keys — and for a minute notice how little of it you decide: its weight, its coolness, its shape. This is not defeat but an honest meeting with scale.

procrastination.text: Baudrillard reproached even Marx for seeing the human being above all as a producer. When you can't get started though you really need to, it's worth recalling this critique before blaming yourself. In The Mirror of Production Baudrillard criticized the notion that a human being is essentially a producer whose value is measured by output. This idea sits so deep in us that we perceive any pause as failure. In The Consumer Society he observed that even rest becomes a duty and a form of working on yourself. Baudrillard might say that procrastination is sometimes not laziness but a quiet bodily “no” to endless mobilization. That doesn't mean the task is unimportant. But if you take off it the weight of being “proof of your worth,” starting often becomes easier. The task is just a task, not a trial of you. You can do a small, ugly, imperfect part of it.
procrastination.practice: Ask your “can't start” as you would ask a striker: what are you on strike against? Hear the answer, then take the tiniest step — just open the file or notebook.

uprooted.text: Death Valley, motels, endless highways — Baudrillard wrote America as a man to whom everything around was foreign. When familiar ground has slipped away after a move or emigration and the old is out of reach, being cut off can run very deep. He traveled a lot and knew that gaze from the inside. In The Transparency of Evil he recalls with sympathy the writer Victor Segalen and his idea of the “exote” — a traveler who is in no hurry to appropriate what is foreign, but learns to value its difference. For Baudrillard, strangeness is not only loss but also a rare experience of meeting something that can't be reduced to yourself. It seems that your foreignness in a new place is painful, but it also holds a sharpness of vision that locals have lost. You see what is invisible to them. You don't have to either dissolve into the new place or cling to the old one: for a while you can simply be in between.
uprooted.practice: Walk around your new place like a foreign photographer: find one detail the locals stopped noticing long ago and study it closely. This is your particular gaze.

overload.text: Picture a radio on which every station in the world plays at once — that is roughly how Baudrillard saw our information environment. Endless feeds, notifications and news are genuinely exhausting, and it isn't about your inability to “cope.” Baudrillard described this state long before smartphones. He called it the “ecstasy of communication”: everything becomes visible, available, instant, and a person turns into a screen through which streams of messages pass. He called this excessive visibility “obscenity” — not in the sense of indecency but in the sense of the disappearance of any stage or distance. Baudrillard would probably note that overload is a normal reaction of a living being to an environment without pauses. Baudrillard also noted the response of “the masses”: not answering, not absorbing, letting things pass by. Sometimes that is the most sensible defense. You don't need to keep up with everything; you can reclaim a stage and a distance — a place where things happen at your own pace.
overload.practice: Mute all notifications for an hour. Meanwhile, do one thing with your hands — wash a cup, water a plant — slowly, as if no other signals existed.

unreality.text: Baudrillard said Disneyland exists to convince us that everything else is real. When the world or you yourself seem not quite real, it can be frightening and disorienting. Baudrillard is perhaps the philosopher who wrote most about a similar experience at the level of culture. In Simulacra and Simulation he describes “hyperreality”: a world where images, models and copies begin to precede reality itself. He recalls Borges's story of a map that grew as large as the empire, and turns it around: now the map precedes the territory. Take Baudrillard's thought one step further, and it turns out that your sense of unreality is not necessarily strange — it resonates with how many people experience life among screens and copies. And yet for Baudrillard reality never disappears completely: traces remain, accidents, the body. You can return to them gently, through the simplest sensations.
unreality.practice: Press your palms together for ten seconds, feeling the warmth and the pressure. Then touch something rough — fabric, a wall, bark — and name aloud what you feel.

quote.text: The territory no longer precedes the map, nor survives it. Henceforth, it is the map that precedes the territory.
quote.author: Jean Baudrillard
quote.source: Simulacra and Simulation (1981), “The Precession of Simulacra”

awe.text: Baudrillard said that in a good photograph it is not he who captures the world, but the world that looks into the lens. Awe before something vast or beautiful is a rare and precious feeling, worth simply living through. Baudrillard, known as a critic of simulations, was also a passionate photographer. He said that in a good photograph the initiative seems to pass to the object itself: it is not we who impose meaning on the world; the world itself comes through and captures us. In America he described deserts as spaces of such scale that familiar meanings dissolve. It follows that awe is the moment when the world exceeds any image or sign, when no picture can contain it. It is the opposite of hyperreality: not a copy, but an encounter with something larger than you. Baudrillard would call it the world's “seduction.” You don't need to do anything with it — it is enough to let yourself be captured.
awe.practice: Stand before something vast — the sky, a tree, the city — and don't take out your phone. Let this be one minute that is in no picture.

relief.text: The exhale after a long “what if” — Baudrillard would explain why it holds so much warmth. When tension lets go, you can simply enjoy the relief. Baudrillard wrote that we often live through events in advance — in images, forecasts, scenarios replayed in our heads — so that the threat becomes almost more real than reality itself. In other words, relief is the moment when this simulation of the future meets the present and turns out not to be the only possibility. And his thought from The Perfect Crime — that the world is never fully calculated — is especially fitting here: things may not follow the worst-case script. Relief shows how much energy you spent on waiting. Let your body feel that this tension can be released — that, too, is a small return to the real.
relief.practice: Take three slow exhales, each longer than the last, and with each one let go of one scenario that never came true.

calm.text: A closed door, a switched-off phone, a cup no one photographs — Baudrillard saw in such small things a rare resistance to the age. Calm comes rarely, and it's good to take care of it. Baudrillard described our world as a space of continuous communication, where everything must be said, shown, discussed. Against this background he valued what remains unsaid: mystery, silence, understatement, which he associated with seduction. Baudrillard might say that calm is a state outside the “ecstasy of communication,” when nothing needs to be broadcast and nothing needs an answer. It demands no result and doesn't become a sign. That is exactly why it is so hard to show to others — and there's no need to. Let your calm stay a little secret. Its value lies not in how it looks but in how it feels.
calm.practice: Sit in silence for five minutes, reporting to no one — not even narrating to yourself how calm you feel. Let the calm stay unpublished.

inspiration.text: Sometimes you don't find an idea — it finds you: in the street, in the shower, in the margins of someone else's book. Baudrillard would take this literally. Baudrillard liked the thought that it is not only the subject who chooses the object; the object also “seduces” the subject: things, images, ideas draw us in by themselves and lead us off the usual path. He connected the very word “seduction” with the Latin se-ducere — “to lead aside.” It seems that inspiration is exactly this kind of seduction, when you are led aside from your schedule and plan. It isn't production on a timetable; it is play. You don't have to turn it into a product right away or report on results. First you can simply follow it — wherever it leads. Inspiration lives in lightness, and it needs no immediate usefulness to be valuable.
inspiration.practice: Go out for ten minutes with no goal and let some object “seduce” you: walk up to whatever caught your eye and study it.

schadenfreude.text: The more insistently a culture smiles, the more unexpectedly its shadows break through — one of Baudrillard's favorite thoughts. A sudden pleasure at someone else's failure doesn't make you a bad person. In The Transparency of Evil Baudrillard writes about “the principle of Evil”: a society that demands constant positivity, agreement and smiles from everyone cannot abolish the negative. It represses it, and then the negative returns in unexpected, strange forms. Baudrillard would probably note that schadenfreude is one of these returns. A world where everyone must look successful and rejoice at others' successes in the feed accumulates hidden tension, and someone else's failure discharges it for a moment. Understanding this doesn't justify cruelty, but it removes some of the shame: your reaction is partly born of an environment of glossy competition. You can notice it without turning it into an action and without punishing yourself for the flash itself.
schadenfreude.practice: Admit it aloud to yourself, briefly and with a smile: “Yes, I'm a little pleased.” A named shadow loses its power — then wish that person something kind.

contempt.text: Baudrillard asked an uncomfortable question: can we bear someone truly unlike us — someone we can neither remake nor fully understand? Contempt feels like calm superiority, but behind it there is often an unwillingness to meet such an other. In The Transparency of Evil Baudrillard writes about “radical otherness” — the other who is truly different from us and can't be reduced to our measures. He believed modern culture tolerates it poorly: the other is either made “the same as us” or cast aside. Baudrillard called this “the hell of the same.” Take Baudrillard's thought one step further, and it turns out that contempt is one way of not letting otherness in: the other is declared “lower,” and then you no longer have to reckon with them. The feeling may have its reasons, and there's no need to shame yourself for it. But it is worth asking: what in this person is so foreign to me that it's easier to devalue them than to be surprised by them?
contempt.practice: Picture the person you despise at a moment when no one is watching: tying their shoelaces, waiting for a bus, tired. Stay with that scene for half a minute.

disgust.text: There is a surfeit that makes you want to turn away, like music played far too loud — Baudrillard saw this state in a whole culture. Disgust at people, a situation or yourself is a strong bodily “no,” and nothing to reproach yourself for. Baudrillard described the modern world as a world of excess: things, images and messages multiply without measure, like “metastases,” and culture reaches a “Xerox degree” — the endless copying of the same thing. He wrote about this with barely hidden disgust at surfeit. It follows that part of disgust comes not from a particular person but from oversaturation: too much, too close, too alike. Then even your own reflection or other people's faces start to set your teeth on edge. In that case disgust is a signal of “enough,” and it's worth listening to: reduce the flow, step away, give yourself some empty space before judging people.
disgust.practice: Go somewhere with few things and few people — a yard, a river, an empty stairwell — and look at empty space for a minute. Let your eyes rest from the “too much.”

revenge.text: A duel at dawn, a return gift, a return visit — Baudrillard saw one ancient logic in them. The wish for revenge says that you were hurt and something inside demands an answer. In Symbolic Exchange and Death Baudrillard describes the “symbolic exchange” on which traditional societies rested: a gift demands a counter-gift, a challenge demands a response. Not responding means remaining humiliated. The modern world, for Baudrillard, has largely destroyed this exchange: often there is no one and nothing with which to answer an injury. In other words, the thirst for revenge is the voice of this ancient need for a response, for restoring balance. It is strong, but it can be quenched not with a blow but with a different kind of answer: naming what happened, defending your boundaries, ending the exchange with the one who wounds you. An answer doesn't have to mirror the injury to give you back your dignity and keep you from being a hostage to someone else's move.
revenge.practice: Come up with a “response” that restores your dignity and harms no one: a calm sentence, a boundary, a refusal. Say it aloud once — for now, just to yourself.

anger_at_loved.text: In the cereal ad, a family has breakfast in a sunny kitchen and nobody raises their voice. Next to such pictures, anger at a partner, parents or children feels especially sharp, and afterward you feel ashamed of it. Baudrillard showed how, in a world of “hyperreality,” images start to seem more real than reality itself. The family has acquired its own simulacra too: perfect family photos, festive dinners, touching posts where no one is ever tired or irritated. Baudrillard might say that next to these images, ordinary family anger seems somehow abnormal. But the glossy family is a copy without an original; it doesn't exist. Real close relationships always include irritation, fatigue and conflict. Anger gives no right to wound, but it doesn't mean your family is “worse.” It means this is real life, not a retouched one.
anger_at_loved.practice: When anger at someone close rises, step into another room for a minute and shake out your hands, shaking off the tension. Come back and say one honest sentence — no advertising script.

ambivalence.text: Baudrillard defended what doesn't fit into plus and minus: the gift, the challenge, ambivalence. Loving someone while being unable to stand them is hard, but it happens very often. In early works such as For a Critique of the Political Economy of the Sign, Baudrillard contrasted two worlds. The world of the “code” demands unambiguity: every thing and every feeling must have a clear value, plus or minus. The world of “symbolic exchange,” for Baudrillard, is by nature ambivalent: gift and threat, love and rivalry are intertwined, and this doubleness can't be neatly sorted out. It seems that mixed feelings toward someone close are a sign of a living, symbolic bond, not of something broken. The demand “make up your mind: do you love them or not?” is the demand of the code. A living bond can be warm and painful at once, and it doesn't need to be reduced to a single number.
ambivalence.practice: Say to yourself one sentence in which both feelings stand side by side without a “but”: “I love you, and I'm angry with you.” Listen to how they coexist.

guilty_relief.text: Baudrillard distrusted scripts written in advance — even the script of “proper” grief. Relief after a breakup, a departure or the death of a seriously ill loved one can be frightening: “how can I feel this?” Relief and love can exist together. Baudrillard described the “precession of simulacra” — a situation where the model precedes reality: first there is a ready-made image, and then a life that is fitted to it. Loss has its models too — films, rituals, the publicly “correct” reactions: only mourning, only tears. Baudrillard would probably note that shame about relief is often born of a mismatch between a living feeling and the model. But the model is not the measure of truth. Real loss is more complex: it can hold exhaustion from long worry and caregiving, release from pain, gratitude and grief all at once. Relief is part of that complexity, not a betrayal.
guilty_relief.practice: Put a hand on your chest and say quietly: “I feel relief, and I love.” Breathe with these words for a minute, without choosing one of the two.

indifference.text: Baudrillard once stood up for those who don't respond: the silent, the non-voting, the indifferent. If you are untouched by what “should” touch you, and guilt follows, his thought can be unexpectedly gentle. In the essay In the Shadow of the Silent Majorities Baudrillard wrote about “the masses,” who are endlessly called upon to respond: vote, worry, sympathize, react. And the masses answer with inertia — silence, indifference, absorbing every message without reply. Baudrillard saw in this not dullness but a peculiar defense against endless mobilization. Take Baudrillard's thought one step further, and it turns out that your indifference is sometimes the same kind of defense: a psyche overloaded with calls to feel temporarily switches off its response. This doesn't mean you are a cold person. Perhaps you need quiet so that your feelings can come back on their own, without being ordered to.
indifference.practice: Allow yourself ten minutes of not feeling anything “properly”: no reacting, no commenting, no likes. Just stay in silence and notice what comes back first.

escape.text: A road straight to the horizon and not a single billboard — that is how Baudrillard remembered the American desert. The urge to drop a job, a city, a role and go where no one knows you says that life has become too cramped or too noisy. In America Baudrillard describes long drives across the American deserts. For him the desert is a space where familiar meanings, roles and social noise vanish, and you can feel pure speed, light, open space. He wrote about it with a traveler's delight. It follows that the pull to escape is a longing for such a “desert”: for a place where signs, expectations and roles don't press on you. This desire doesn't necessarily require moving away. Sometimes it's enough to find your own small “desert” — a time and place where for an hour you are free of roles.
escape.practice: Step away for five minutes into your own “desert”: a balcony, a stairwell, an empty street, without your phone. Notice what changes in you without roles.

forbidden_attraction.text: For Baudrillard, seduction is a game, not a command: it beckons, but demands nothing be carried out. An attraction to someone unavailable or “the wrong” person can be confusing and frightening. But a feeling is not an act. In Seduction Baudrillard reminds us that the Latin root of “seduction” means “to lead aside,” to lead off the straight path. He contrasted seduction with “production”: seduction is a play of signs, of the unsaid, of distance, not the uncovering of some “truth of desire.” He even argued with psychoanalysis, which sees in every attraction a secret truth about a person. In other words, a forbidden attraction doesn't necessarily say “here is your true desire, act on it.” It may be a game that leads you aside from the familiar and shows what you are missing. You can look at it with interest without turning it into either a verdict or a program.
forbidden_attraction.practice: Look at this attraction as if it were a dream: what in it beckons — lightness, attention, novelty? Name it in one word and look for a grain of it in your current life.

social_anxiety.text: Before meeting people you seem to be preparing a photograph rather than a conversation — a very Baudrillardian situation. Fear of judgment is exhausting and turns every conversation into an exam. Baudrillard showed that in the age of “hyperreality” people increasingly meet each other's images rather than each other: retouched photos, carefully calibrated posts, confident public selves. These images seem more real than the people themselves. Baudrillard might say that part of social anxiety comes from comparison: you know your own life from the inside, with all its doubts, while you see others through their smooth simulacra. It seems everyone around is confident and only you are not. But this is a comparison of a living person with a copy without an original. Behind other people's confident images there are also worries, stumbles, awkwardness. You are not the only one who is nervous.
social_anxiety.practice: In your next conversation, ask the person one simple question and listen to the answer, not to your own reflection. Notice something alive in them — a gesture, a stumble, a laugh in their voice.

uncertainty.text: A month-ahead weather forecast gets it wrong, and Baudrillard would see in this not a failure of science but a property of the world. Uncertainty is hard: you want to know what will happen, and you can't. In late books such as Impossible Exchange, Baudrillard wrote about the “radical uncertainty” of the world: the world can never be fully exchanged for meaning, reduced to a model, a forecast, an explanation. He believed that attempts to calculate and insure against everything only make life more anxious, because uncertainty remains anyway. It seems that your uncertainty is not a personal failure of planning but a property of the world itself, one everyone faces. This doesn't make the waiting easier, but it relieves you of a task no one can manage: foreseeing everything. You can live inside uncertainty, leaning on what is here now.
uncertainty.practice: Toss a coin and, while it's in the air, notice how your body wants to know the answer. Then don't look at how it landed — just put it in your pocket.

waiting.text: Two grey ticks have turned blue, and still no reply: Baudrillard would call this the tyranny of “real time.” Waiting for results, a reply or news stretches time, and it's hard to find your place in it. In The Illusion of the End Baudrillard wrote about the culture of “real time”: everything must happen instantly, with no delay, distance or pause. The message has been delivered — so the answer must come now. Baudrillard would probably note that waiting has become especially painful for us precisely because we have lost the habit of waiting: any pause feels like a glitch, a catastrophe. But many things — decisions, results, other people's answers — have their own time, which doesn't match the time of the screen. Waiting is not a breakdown but a return to a human rhythm. You can live through it without checking every minute whether it has arrived yet.
waiting.practice: Set a timer for three minutes and spend it looking out of the window — at clouds, passers-by, branches. Let the pause be not a glitch but a small space that belongs to you.

regret.text: Baudrillard would ask your “what if I had chosen differently?”: where is the original of that other life? Regret over what you did or didn't do can return again and again. Baudrillard wrote about simulacra — copies that have no original. Take Baudrillard's thought one step further, and it turns out that the “other life” regret paints resembles such a simulacrum. It never existed, and so it is flawless: it has none of the boredom, mistakes and random misfortunes that would have been on the other path too. You are comparing a lived, living life with a perfect copy of what never happened — and the living life loses. It's an unfair comparison. Yet regret can speak of something real: of values that matter to you. You can take them out of the imagined life and begin to live them in the real one, with all its rough edges.
regret.practice: In the spirit of Baudrillard's Cool Memories, write one aphorism about your regret — a single sentence, ironic and precise. Read it aloud.

longing.text: Copies increasingly replace the real — Baudrillard spent half his life on this thought, but there is one feeling that resists it. You can miss a particular person — their voice, their smell, their presence — almost physically. Today we have photos, videos, messages, video calls — an almost complete illusion of presence. And still the longing doesn't pass. It follows that longing is precisely the feeling of the reality that can't be simulated: a body present beside you, a shared silence, a touch. A copy can remind you of a person but not replace them. In this sense your longing is faithfulness to the real. You can use images to stay in touch without blaming yourself that they aren't enough: they can't be enough.
longing.practice: Recall one touch or scent of this person that no photo holds. Hold that memory in your body for a minute — it is yours, and it can't be copied.

world_pain.text: Baudrillard wouldn't ask what you think about the news — he would ask whether you can answer it in any way at all. Pain for the world from heavy news, wars and injustice can weigh you down, and it speaks of your sensitivity. In the essay “Requiem for the Media” Baudrillard observed that the media are built as “speech without response”: they talk to us, show us everything, but we can barely answer. In other words, pain for the world is especially heavy not only because of the events themselves but because of this one-sidedness: you see suffering but can't respond to it. Tension builds up with nowhere to go. That's why it helps to reclaim at least a small response: not just to watch, but to do something — help, support, talk. Even a small response breaks the one-way flow and gives you back your voice.
world_pain.practice: Today, talk with one person about what troubles you in the world — no arguing, just say it and listen. A conversation between two gives you back your voice; then set the news aside until tomorrow.

rejection.text: A product on the shelf doesn't know why it wasn't picked: it was simply compared with its neighbor on a few features. Baudrillard showed that the system treats people this way too, turning them into sets of signs — which is why rejection stings: it feels as if you were assessed and found insufficient. Today you can see this, for example, in dating apps and job selection: a decision is made in seconds based on a few features — a photo, a line on a résumé. Baudrillard might say that many rejections concern not you but your “sign,” the tiny image that passed through someone else's filter. That image never coincides with the living person. The pain of rejection is real, but it doesn't prove you are “not enough.” What was rejected was a sign, not your complex, real self.
rejection.practice: Name aloud three things about you that can't be seen in a photo or on a résumé: how you laugh, how you comfort, what you remember. No filter has weighed these.

abandonment.text: An object in a collection will never leave, but a person can: Baudrillard saw in this both the pain and the gift of a living bond. The fear of being abandoned is exhausting — you catch every sign and dread every pause — and this fear, often grown from old wounds, deserves gentleness. In The System of Objects Baudrillard writes about collecting. He notes that objects also attract us because they can be completely controlled: a collection will never leave, never fall out of love, never abandon you. Through objects a person tries to cope with the fear of loss. It seems that the fear of being abandoned is the other side of the fact that a living person will never become an “object” in our collection. They are free — and so they can leave. But that is exactly why their presence beside you is not possession but a choice they make. You can notice that choice and value it.
abandonment.practice: Recall today's sign that someone close chose to be with you: a message, a glance, a cup of tea. Tell them — just “I noticed.”

unrequited.text: The artist Sophie Calle secretly followed a stranger all the way to Venice, and Baudrillard wrote an essay about it: you can follow another as long as you like and never possess them. When you give your feeling and no answer comes, it wounds deeply. In Fatal Strategies Baudrillard offers an unexpected view: we usually think that the subject — the one who desires — is in charge, and the object is passive. But Baudrillard shows that the object is often stronger: it slips away, doesn't respond, remains impenetrable, and precisely by doing so holds our attention. Baudrillard would probably note that in unrequited love the other is not “to blame” and not “cruel”: they simply remain other and don't submit to our desire. This is hard to accept, but it frees you from the endless attempt to “earn” an answer. Your feeling is real and valuable, but you are not obliged to pursue someone who remains beyond your power.
unrequited.practice: Go for a short walk and in your mind let that person go their own way, like a stranger in the crowd. Your feeling stays with you — and it is yours.

humiliation.text: Baudrillard defended something that has almost vanished today — the right not to be fully visible. When you want a scene erased from memory, yours and everyone else's, that right feels especially precious: humiliation is one of the most painful experiences. Baudrillard wrote about the “transparency” of the modern world: everything must be visible; everything is recorded, forwarded, discussed. An awkward moment can turn into a picture that lives separately from you. Take Baudrillard's thought one step further, and it turns out that a humiliating scene, especially one many people saw, turns into a simulacrum — an image that seems more real than you yourself. But it is a copy of a single moment cut out of a life. You are not that scene. You have a past before it and a future after it that the image can't contain. In time, other people's attention moves on to new pictures, and you remain yourself.
humiliation.practice: Replay that scene in your imagination like someone else's film, then shrink the screen to the size of a postage stamp and push it into a corner of the room. You are bigger than that frame.

body_shame.text: A mannequin in a shop window never tires, never ages, never breathes — it simply has no life to carry. A quiet, constant dissatisfaction with your body deserves care, and Baudrillard helps explain where it comes from. Symbolic Exchange and Death has a chapter called “The Body, or the Mass Grave of Signs.” Baudrillard shows how fashion and advertising cut the body into separate “parts-as-signs”: lips, legs, belly, skin — each part must meet a standard and is judged separately. It follows that body shame often works the same way: you look not at yourself as a whole but at a “detail” that “falls short.” But the body is not a set of signs; it is a living whole that breathes, moves, feels and holds you in the world. You can return from examining parts to sensing yourself as a whole.
body_shame.practice: Walk slowly around the room, feeling your body from inside — weight, step, the warmth of your palms — not from outside, in the mirror. Tell it: “Thank you for carrying me.”

illness.text: A fitness band counts your steps and cheers you on, and when you're lying in bed with a fever it seems to reproach you silently. Baudrillard would explain where that reproach comes from: when the body lets you down, it is hard physically and emotionally, and plans fall apart. In The Consumer Society Baudrillard wrote about the “cult of health”: health becomes not simply a good but an obligation and a status symbol. A healthy, toned, energetic body is the mark of a successful person. In other words, in such a world illness is experienced not only as suffering but as a “failure,” a shameful defeat. This adds extra weight to what is already hard. But illness is not a failure or a sign of your inadequacy. It is part of human life, something that happens to all bodies. You can release yourself from the demand to “keep it together” and let yourself simply be ill and take care of yourself.
illness.practice: For today, take off the role of the “energetic, toned person” — at least aloud: “Today I am simply ill.” Choose one small act of care for yourself, with no demand to be productive.

pride.text: Baudrillard loved things that carry a history rather than just a price. Pride in what you've made yourself is a healthy, well-earned feeling, and it is worth enjoying. In The System of Objects Baudrillard compares mass-produced, assembly-line objects with antique, handmade ones. An antique object, he observes, has a special value: you can see in it “the trace of the hand,” the imprint of the person who made it. Baudrillard might say that healthy pride is joy in such a trace: not in a “status symbol” that can be bought, but in having made something yourself, having put in time, effort and attention. Such pride can't be faked or purchased. It needs no display or likes, though sharing it with people close to you is good too. You can simply look at what you've made and recognize your own hand in it.
pride.practice: Take in your hands something you made (or recall it) and find its “trace of the hand” — the place where your effort shows. Let your gaze rest there.

melancholy.text: Baudrillard often photographed empty streets, windows, peeling walls — pictures with almost no people but plenty of quiet light. A gentle sadness with no misfortune in it is in tune with them: it doesn't need “fixing.” In the final chapter of Simulacra and Simulation Baudrillard wrote about melancholy as the general mood of the era: a world where meanings dissolve in a stream of images is tinged with quiet sadness. He said this about culture, not about individuals, but something warm can be drawn from his thought. It seems that a personal, gentle melancholy is a way of feeling the real amid the gloss. It doesn't put on a brave face or fake positivity, and it lets you notice fragility, time gone by, real losses. In this sense melancholy is an honest feeling. You can live through it without shame, allowing yourself a little silence and shadow.
melancholy.practice: Find a corner of quiet light in the room or outside the window and simply look at it for two minutes, taking no picture. Let the sadness stay beside you, like that light.
